# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

HTTP 200
Texas Criminal Illegal Noncitizen Data | Department of Public Safety 

 Skip to main content

 Texas Criminal Illegal Noncitizen Data 

 August 27, 2020 

 The Department of Public Safety and local law enforcement agencies in Texas participate in the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Secure Communities.  Participation in Secure Communities enables DHS to work with state and local law enforcement to take custody of individuals who pose a danger to public safety before those individuals are released into our communities.  In Texas, Secure Communities begins at the local level when an individual is arrested and booked by a Texas law enforcement officer for a criminal violation of Texas law.  The arrested individual’s fingerprints are submitted to the Texas DPS and subsequently to the FBI for criminal history and warrant checks. This same biometric data is also sent to DHS’ IDENT database so that ICE can determine the person’s immigration status and whether the individual is a priority for removal, consistent with the DHS enforcement priorities.  The immigration status information is returned to DPS by DHS.  The following report is based upon the status indicators provided to the DPS.  For the purposes of this report, the term “criminal noncitizens” refers to an individual who has been identified as a noncitizen by DHS and who has been arrested for a state criminal offense, typically a Misdemeanor B or higher, committed in Texas. 
 Lawful Presence Determined Through Secure Communities 
 According to DHS status indicators, over 466,000 criminal noncitizens have been booked into local Texas jails between June 1, 2011, and September 30, 2026, of which over 335,000 were classified as illegal noncitizens by DHS.
 Between June 1, 2011, and September 30, 2026, these 335,000 illegal noncitizens were charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses which included arrests for 1,134 homicide charges; 79,089 assault charges; 10,669 burglary charges;   70,672 drug charges; 1,547 kidnapping charges; 30,692 theft charges; 48,105 obstructing police charges; 3,424 robbery charges; 7,713 sexual assault charges; 8,733 sexual offense charges; and 7,669 weapon charges.   DPS criminal history records reflect those criminal charges have thus far resulted in over 230,000 convictions including 636 homicide convictions; 29,993 assault convictions; 5,564 burglary convictions; 29,414 drug convictions; 463 kidnapping convictions; 11,900 theft convictions; 18,758 obstructing police convictions; 2,040 robbery convictions; 4,025 sexual assault convictions; 4,074 sexual offense convictions; and 2,543 weapon convictions. 

 Enlarge chart 
 These figures only count individuals who previously had an encounter with DHS that resulted in their fingerprints being entered into the DHS IDENT database.   Foreign nationals who enter the country illegally and avoid detection by DHS but are later arrested by local or state law enforcement for a state offense will not have a DHS response in regard to their lawful status and do not appear in these counts.   However, in addition to the Secure Communities program, DHS actively adjudicates the immigration status of individuals incarcerated in the Texas prison system.   From 2011 to date, the Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) has provided DPS with information on more than 35,000 individuals who were identified by DHS as in the country illegally while they were incarcerated at TDCJ.   11,000 of these individuals were not identified through the Secure Communities program at the time of their arrest.   DPS does not know the current incarceration status of the individuals identified while they were incarcerated nor when their noncitizen status was initially determined.
 Lawful Presence Determined While Incarcerated at TDCJ
 Between June 1, 2011 and September 30, 2026, these 11,000 individual identified as illegal noncitizens while in prison, but who were not previously identified through Secure Communities, were charged with more than 12,000 criminal offenses which included arrests for 156 homicide charges; 1,672 assault charges; 636 burglary charges; 2,117 drug charges; 77 kidnapping charges; 599 theft charges; 1,195 obstructing police charges; 474 robbery charges; 1,025 sexual assault charges; 499 sexual offense charges; and 313 weapon charges.   DPS criminal history records reflect those criminal charges have thus far resulted in over 6,000 convictions including 120 homicide convictions; 964 assault convictions; 404 burglary convictions; 1,149 drug convictions; 41 kidnapping convictions; 330 theft convictions; 518 obstructing police convictions; 351 robbery convictions; 745 sexual assault convictions; 356 sexual offense convictions; and 124 weapon convictions.   

 Enlarge chart 
 Because DPS does not know the date these individuals were identified as illegal while in prison, the count of charges for which this population was arrested between June 1, 2011, and September 30, 2026, does not necessarily align with the size of the population of illegal noncitizens identified while in prison.  A more accurate assessment can be seen when examining this population’s entire Texas criminal history and not just for offenses committed during this time period (see the Historical Data section of this report).  However, for this report, in order to be consistent with the timeframe utilized to provide counts of arrest and conviction for the population identified through Secure Communities, we have limited the arrest and conviction counts for prison identified illegal noncitizens to the same June 1, 2011, to September 30, 2026, time frame used for individuals identified through Secure Communities. 
 Report Notes 
 These figures do not attempt to allege that foreign nationals in the country illegally commit more crimes than other groups. It simply identifies thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims that should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here. It is also important to note that these figures represent the minimum number of crimes associated with criminal illegal noncitizens:
 These figures only count arrests in Texas for state offenses.  These individuals may have criminal records in other states.
 These figures only represent offenses and convictions that are associated with arrest events that occurred between June 1, 2011, and September 30, 2026.
 The criminal activity for individuals identified as illegal while in prison is under represented for this time period because they may have been incarcerated during the time frame used in this report.
 These figures do not count federal criminal charges.
 These figures do not include similar data for foreign nationals who are lawfully in the country and commit state criminal offenses.
 Individuals whose lawful presence was determined while in prison may or may not be currently incarcerated.

HTTP 200
Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org 

 Skip to main content 

 FactCheck .org ® 

 A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center 

 This article is available in both English and Español 
 English 
 Español 

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

 A: No. An Ohio mental health center rebutted false online rumors that Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, had been there as a patient. Talarico said he was off the campaign trail for several days in early October while recovering from the flu at his Texas home.

{"content": "# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 alone. New York has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley as she ran on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. ICE reports that Ibarra entered the country illegally in September 2022 and that the New York Police Department released him after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. A Georgia judge sent him to prison for life. Riley's death was preventable, and the federal government knew exactly who Ibarra was.

Her case is not an anomaly. It is the predictable result of a system that identifies criminal aliens and then releases them. ICE's non-detained docket is the roster of removable aliens the agency is not holding. As of July 21, 2024, that roster included 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, among them 13,099 with homicide convictions and another 1,845 awaiting trial on homicide charges. In plain terms, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Every line of that docket is a policy choice. The alien was identified. The conviction is on the books. The removal authority exists. What is missing is detention capacity and the will to use it. Congress does not need new statistics to act on this docket. It needs to fund the beds.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same story is written in federal sentencing data. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced that year, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable from the country.

Two-thirds of these noncitizen offenders, 65.9%, came from Mexico, followed by Honduras (8.7%) and Guatemala (5.8%). Illegal aliens are not a rounding error in the federal criminal caseload. They are more than a third of it, and each of those sentences stands for a crime with a victim.

These figures count federal convictions only. The state caseloads are larger, and one state keeps the records that allow the public to see them clearly.

## 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records immigration status in its criminal justice data, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety records the best available window on illegal alien crime at the state level. The view is grim. From June 1, 2011, through Sept. 30, 2026, Texas booked more than 466,000 criminal noncitizens into its jails. More than 335,000 of them were classified by DHS as illegal noncitizens, and they were charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses, including 1,134 homicide charges, 79,089 assault charges, 7,713 sexual assault charges, 10,669 burglary charges and 70,672 drug charges. Those charges have so far produced more than 230,000 convictions, including 636 homicide convictions.

DPS describes its own numbers as thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims who should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here. The agency also notes that its counts include only aliens whose fingerprints were already on file with DHS, which means the true totals are higher.

Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies, examining the same Texas records, conclude that identification delays understate illegal alien criminality even now, and that illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the general population. Texas DPS data are the floor, not the ceiling.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

How does a convicted criminal alien stay out of ICE custody long enough to reoffend? Ask the sanctuary jurisdictions. A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after a scheduled release so that federal officers can take custody. Sanctuary policies order local jails not to comply. In calendar 2025, jurisdictions across the country declined 17,864 ICE detainers, according to DHS testimony to Congress in March 2026.

New York is the case study. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, the state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers. The criminal charges and convictions associated with those refusals total 52,503, including 131 homicide charges and convictions, 1,017 sexual offenses, 1,776 robberies and 9,502 assaults. DHS has documented the results: illegal aliens released despite detainers have gone on to murder, rape and rob in the very communities that sheltered them. Rather than change course, New York enacted a 2026 law barring local police departments from partnering with ICE.

Congress has answered once already. The Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, requires the detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary or assaulting a law enforcement officer. It is named for a victim the system failed. It should not be the last such law.

## 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund the detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the detention capacity ICE needs to take custody of the 425,431 convicted criminals on its docket, with homicide and violent convictions first in line.
2. **Enforce detainer compliance.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers, and extend the Laken Riley Act's mandatory detention standard to illegal aliens charged with any violent felony.
3. **Expand 287(g).** ICE has signed 2,679 agreements with state and local law enforcement agencies across 38 states. Fund the program so that every willing agency can participate.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly data on the non-detained docket, on detainers declined by jurisdiction, and on every release of a criminal alien from custody.

The data in this brief are the government's own. The question before Congress is whether it will act on them before the next victim's name is written into law.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. The data appendix to this brief (tables A1-A5) accompanies this publication.*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | October 2026

**Executive summary**
- ICE's own docket data show that 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions refused 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025. New York alone has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

**1. The Non-Detained Docket**

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien and Tren de Aragua gang member, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley on the University of Georgia campus. ICE says Ibarra had entered the country illegally in September 2022 and was released by the New York Police Department after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. He is now serving life without parole. Riley would be alive today if the system had held a criminal alien it had already identified.

Ibarra's case is not an outlier; it is the policy. ICE's non-detained docket is the list of removable aliens the agency is not holding, and the government's own numbers describe the scale: as of July 21, 2024, the docket held 425,431 convicted criminals. Among them are 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions. Another 1,845 face homicide charges. The house line: 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Argument paragraph: These are not statistics; they are preventable victims... ICE does not have the beds to hold them; policy that releases criminal aliens after identification... Every vacancy on the docket is a choice by Washington.

**2. Federal Sentencing**

The same pattern shows up at sentencing. Per USSC Quick Facts FY2024: more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced in fiscal 2024. 88.7% of them were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens. Country of origin: 65.9% Mexico, 8.7% Honduras, 5.8% Guatemala, 4.0% Dominican Republic, 3.0% El Salvador. Argument: illegal aliens are not a marginal part of the federal criminal caseload; they are over a third of it. Every one of those sentences represents a crime that had a victim... And note: these are federal sentences only; state systems carry far more. Which the Texas data show.

**3. State Data: Texas**

Texas DPS is the only state agency that systematically records immigration status... From June 1, 2011 through Sept. 30, 2026: more than 466,000 criminal noncitizens booked into Texas jails; over 335,000 confirmed illegal noncitizens; charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses — including 1,134 homicide charges, 79,089 assault charges, 7,713 sexual assault charges, 10,669 burglary charges and 70,672 drug charges. Convictions thus far: over 230,000, including 636 homicide convictions.
DPS framing: "thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims that should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here." DPS counts only aliens previously identified in DHS databases → the numbers are a floor, not a ceiling.
Center for Immigration Studies: identification delays mean official counts understate illegal-alien criminality; analysts conclude illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the general population in Texas.

**4. Sanctuary Policies and Detainers**

How do convicted criminal aliens stay out of ICE custody? Sanctuary policies. A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien up to 48 hours for pickup. Sanctuary jurisdictions order their jails not to comply. In calendar 2025, jurisdictions nationwide declined 17,864 detainers. New York: between Jan. 20, 2025 and Oct. 8, 2026, 16,070 detainers not honored; the associated criminal charges and convictions total 52,503, including 131 homicides, 1,017 sexual offenses, 1,776 robberies and 9,502 assaults. And rather than change, New York enacted a law in 2026 barring local police from cooperating with ICE. Congress answered the Riley case once — the Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1), signed Jan. 29, 2025, mandates detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assaulting law enforcement... It is the model; it needs successors.

**5. Recommendations to Congress**

1. Fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket. Congress should appropriate the detention capacity ICE needs to take custody of the 425,431 convicted criminals now on the docket, prioritizing homicide and violence convictions. 3. Expand 287(g). ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements covering 38 states; fund the program so every willing sheriff's office can participate. 
4. Require public reporting. Require DHS to publish quarterly data on the non-detained docket, declined detainers by jurisdiction, and every release of a criminal alien.

Closing line: The data are the government's own. The question is whether Congress will act on them before the next name becomes a law's title.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 alone. New York has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

### 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley as she ran on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. ICE reports that Ibarra entered the country illegally in September 2022 and that the New York Police Department released him after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. A Georgia judge sent him to prison for life. Riley's death was preventable, and the federal government knew exactly who Ibarra was.

Her case is not an anomaly. It is the predictable result of a system that identifies criminal aliens and then releases them. ICE's non-detained docket is the roster of removable aliens the agency is not holding. As of July 21, 2024, that roster included 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, among them 13,099 with homicide convictions and another 1,845 awaiting trial on homicide charges. In plain terms, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Every line of that docket is a policy choice. The alien was identified; the conviction is on the books; the removal authority exists. What is missing is detention capacity and the will to use it. Congress does not need new statistics to act on this docket. It needs to fund the beds.

### 2. Federal sentencing

The same story is written in federal sentencing data. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced that year, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

Two-thirds of these offenders, 65.9%, came from Mexico, followed by Honduras (8.7%) and Guatemala (5.8%). Illegal aliens are not a rounding error in the federal criminal caseload. They are more than a third of it, and each of those sentences stands for a crime with a victim.

These figures count federal convictions only. The state data are larger, and one state keeps the records that let us see them clearly.

### 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of people it books and convicts, which makes its Department of Public Safety data the best available window on illegal alien crime at the state level. The window is grim. From June 1, 2011, through Sept. 30, 2026, Texas booked more than 466,000 criminal noncitizens into its jails. More than 335,000 of them were classified by DHS as illegal noncitizens, and they were charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses: 1,134 homicide charges, 79,089 assault charges, 7,713 sexual assault charges, 10,669 burglary charges and 70,672 drug charges. Those charges have so far produced more than 230,000 convictions, including 636 homicide convictions.

DPS describes its own numbers as thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims who should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here. The agency also notes that these counts include only aliens whose fingerprints were already in DHS databases, which means the true totals are higher.

Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies, examining the same Texas records, conclude that identification delays mean official counts understate illegal alien criminality still further, and that illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the general population. Texas DPS data are the floor, not the ceiling.

### 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

How does a convicted criminal alien stay out of ICE custody long enough to reoffend? Ask the sanctuary jurisdictions. A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after scheduled release so federal officers can take custody. Sanctuary policies order local jails not to comply. In calendar 2025, jurisdictions across the country declined 17,864 detainers, according to DHS testimony to Congress in March 2026.

New York is the case study. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, the state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers. The criminal charges and convictions associated with those refused detainers total 52,503, including 131 homicides, 1,017 sexual offenses, 1,776 robberies and 9,502 assaults. DHS documents the results: illegal aliens released despite detainers have gone on to murder, rape and rob in the very communities that sheltered them. Rather than change course, New York enacted a 2026 law barring local police departments from partnering with ICE.

Congress has answered once already. The Laken Riley Act, the first legislation signed into law in 2025, requires the detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary or assaulting a law enforcement officer. It is named for a victim the system failed. It should not be the last such law.

### 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund the detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the detention capacity ICE needs to take custody of the 425,431 convicted criminals on its docket, with homicide and violent convictions first in line.
2. **Enforce detainer compliance.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers, and extend the Laken Riley Act's mandatory detention standard to illegal aliens charged with any violent felony.
3. **Expand 287(g).** ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state and local agencies across 38 states. Fund the program so that every willing law enforcement agency can participate.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly data on the non-detained docket, on detainers declined by jurisdiction, and on every release of a criminal alien from custody.

The data in this brief are the government's own. The question before Congress is whether it will act on them before the next victim's name is written into law.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. Data appendix available [with the brief].*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | October 2026

**Executive summary**
- ICE's own docket data show that 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions refused 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025. New York alone has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

**1. The Non-Detained Docket**

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien and Tren de Aragua gang member, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley on the University of Georgia campus. ICE says Ibarra had entered the country illegally in September 2022 and was released by the New York Police Department after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. He is now serving life without parole. Riley would be alive today if the system had held a criminal alien it had already identified.

Ibarra's case is not an outlier; it is the policy. ICE's non-detained docket is the list of removable aliens the agency is not holding, and the government's own numbers describe the scale: as of July 21, 2024, the docket held 425,431 convicted criminals. Among them are 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions. Another 1,845 face homicide charges. The house line: 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Argument paragraph: These are not statistics; they are preventable victims... ICE does not have the beds to hold them; policy that releases criminal aliens after identification... Every vacancy on the docket is a choice by Washington.

Per USSC Quick Facts FY2024: more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced in fiscal 2024. 88.7% of them were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens. # Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14
## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 alone. New York has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

### 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley as she ran on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. ICE reports that Ibarra entered the country illegally in September 2022 and that the New York Police Department released him after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. A Georgia judge sent him to prison for life. Riley's death was preventable, and the federal government knew exactly who Ibarra was.

Her case is not an anomaly. It is the predictable result of a system that identifies criminal aliens and then releases them. ICE's non-detained docket is the roster of removable aliens the agency is not holding. As of July 21, 2024, that roster included 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, among them 13,099 with homicide convictions and another 1,845 awaiting trial on homicide charges. In plain terms, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Every line of that docket is a policy choice. The alien was identified; the conviction is on the books; the removal authority exists. What is missing is detention capacity and the will to use it. Congress does not need new statistics to act on this docket. It needs to fund the beds.

### 2. Federal sentencing

The same story is written in federal sentencing data. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced that year, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

Two-thirds of these offenders, 65.9%, came from Mexico, followed by Honduras (8.7%) and Guatemala (5.8%). Illegal aliens are not a rounding error in the federal criminal caseload. They are more than a third of it, and each of those sentences stands for a crime with a victim.

These figures count federal convictions only. The state data are larger, and one state keeps the records that let us see them clearly.

### 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of people it books and convicts, which makes its Department of Public Safety data the best available window on illegal alien crime at the state level. The window is grim. From June 1, 2011, through Sept. 30, 2026, Texas booked more than 466,000 criminal noncitizens into its jails. More than 335,000 of them were classified by DHS as illegal noncitizens, and they were charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses: 1,134 homicide charges, 79,089 assault charges, 7,713 sexual assault charges, 10,669 burglary charges and 70,672 drug charges. Those charges have so far produced more than 230,000 convictions, including 636 homicide convictions.

DPS describes its own numbers as thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims who should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here. The agency also notes that these counts include only aliens whose fingerprints were already in DHS databases, which means the true totals are higher.

Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies, examining the same Texas records, conclude that identification delays mean official counts understate illegal alien criminality still further, and that illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the general population. Texas DPS data are the floor, not the ceiling.

### 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

How does a convicted criminal alien stay out of ICE custody long enough to reoffend? Ask the sanctuary jurisdictions. A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after scheduled release so federal officers can take custody. Sanctuary policies order local jails not to comply. In calendar 2025, jurisdictions across the country declined 17,864 detainers, according to DHS testimony to Congress in March 2026.

New York is the case study. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, the state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers. The criminal charges and convictions associated with those refused detainers total 52,503, including 131 homicides, 1,017 sexual offenses, 1,776 robberies and 9,502 assaults. DHS documents the results: illegal aliens released despite detainers have gone on to murder, rape and rob in the very communities that sheltered them. Rather than change course, New York enacted a 2026 law barring local police departments from partnering with ICE.

Congress has answered once already. The Laken Riley Act, the first legislation signed into law in 2025, requires the detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary or assaulting a law enforcement officer. It is named for a victim the system failed. It should not be the last such law.

### 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund the detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the detention capacity ICE needs to take custody of the 425,431 convicted criminals on its docket, with homicide and violent convictions first in line.
2. **Enforce detainer compliance.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers, and extend the Laken Riley Act's mandatory detention standard to illegal aliens charged with any violent felony.
3. **Expand 287(g).** ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state and local agencies across 38 states. Fund the program so that every willing law enforcement agency can participate.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly data on the non-detained docket, on detainers declined by jurisdiction, and on every release of a criminal alien from custody.

The data in this brief are the government's own. The question before Congress is whether it will act on them before the next victim's name is written into law.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. Data appendix available [with the brief].*

{"content": "# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 alone. New York has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley as she ran on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. ICE reports that Ibarra entered the country illegally in September 2022 and that the New York Police Department released him after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. A Georgia judge sent him to prison for life. Riley's death was preventable, and the federal government knew exactly who Ibarra was.

Her case is not an anomaly. It is the predictable result of a system that identifies criminal aliens and then releases them. ICE's non-detained docket is the roster of removable aliens the agency is not holding. As of July 21, 2024, that roster included 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, among them 13,099 with homicide convictions and another 1,845 awaiting trial on homicide charges. In plain terms, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Every line of that docket is a policy choice. The alien was identified. The conviction is on the books. The removal authority exists. What is missing is detention capacity and the will to use it. Congress sets ICE's detention capacity in annual appropriations, so every murderer on that docket rather than in a bed is a decision made in Washington, not an accident of the system. The agency does not need new statistics to act on this docket. It needs the funding and the mandate.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same story is written in federal sentencing data. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced that year, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable from the country.

Two-thirds of these noncitizen offenders, 65.9%, came from Mexico, followed by Honduras (8.7%) and Guatemala (5.8%). Illegal aliens are not a rounding error in the federal criminal caseload. They are more than a third of it, and each of those sentences stands for a crime with a victim. A noncitizen who reaches a federal sentencing hearing has already been arrested, charged and convicted in an American courtroom. Removal at that point should be automatic. Instead, criminal aliens complete their sentences, cycle back into communities and reappear on dockets like the one described above.

These figures count federal convictions only. The state caseloads are larger, and one state keeps the records that allow the public to see them clearly.

## 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records immigration status in its criminal justice data, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety records the best available window on illegal alien crime at the state level. The view is grim. From June 1, 2011, through Sept. 30, 2026, Texas booked more than 466,000 criminal noncitizens into its jails. More than 335,000 of them were classified by DHS as illegal noncitizens, and they were charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses, including 1,134 homicide charges, 79,089 assault charges, 7,713 sexual assault charges, 10,669 burglary charges, 1,547 kidnapping charges and 70,672 drug charges. Those charges have so far produced more than 230,000 convictions, including 636 homicide convictions.

DPS describes its own numbers as thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims who should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here. The agency also notes that its counts include only aliens whose fingerprints were already on file with DHS, which means the true totals are higher.

The data themselves show how much higher. Texas has identified more than 11,000 illegal noncitizens only after they were already behind bars, too late for any detainer to matter, and that group alone carries 156 homicide charges and 120 homicide convictions. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies, examining the same Texas records, conclude that these identification delays understate illegal alien criminality even now, and that illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the general population. Texas DPS data are the floor, not the ceiling.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

How does a convicted criminal alien stay out of ICE custody long enough to reoffend? Ask the sanctuary jurisdictions. A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after a scheduled release so that federal officers can take custody. Sanctuary policies order local jails not to comply. In calendar 2025, jurisdictions across the country declined 17,864 ICE detainers, according to DHS testimony to Congress in March 2026.

New York is the case study. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, the state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers. The criminal charges and convictions associated with those refusals total 52,503, including 131 homicide charges and convictions, 1,017 sexual offenses, 1,776 robberies and 9,502 assaults. In December 2025, ICE's acting director wrote to New York's attorney general that sanctuary policies had freed nearly 7,000 criminal illegal aliens, including murderers and sexual predators. DHS has documented the results: a Queens murder and arson case in which the city's Department of Correction refused a detainer, and a Huntington rape case involving a 16-year-old victim. Rather than change course, New York enacted a 2026 law barring local police departments from partnering with ICE.

Congress has answered once already. The Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, requires the detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary or assaulting a law enforcement officer. It is named for a victim the system failed. It should not be the last such law.

## 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund the detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the detention capacity ICE needs to take custody of the 425,431 convicted criminals on its docket, with homicide and violent convictions first in line, and report back on the docket's size each quarter.
2. **Enforce detainer compliance.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers, and extend the Laken Riley Act's mandatory detention standard to illegal aliens charged with any violent felony.
3. **Expand 287(g).** ICE has signed 2,679 agreements with state and local law enforcement agencies across 38 states. Fund the program so that every willing agency can participate, and let states require their sheriffs to cooperate.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly data on the non-detained docket, on detainers declined by jurisdiction, and on every release of a criminal alien from custody. What gets measured gets enforced.

The data in this brief are the government's own. The question before Congress is whether it will act on them before the next victim's name is written into law.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. The data appendix to this brief (tables A1-A5) accompanies this publication.*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE data show 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities, part of a non-detained docket that includes 425,431 convicted criminals.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 alone. New York has ignored 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

## 1. The non-detained docket

On Feb. 22, 2024, Jose Ibarra, a Venezuelan illegal alien, murdered 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley as she ran on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. ICE reports that Ibarra entered the country illegally in September 2022 and that the New York Police Department released him after an August 2023 arrest, before ICE could take him into custody. A Georgia judge sent him to prison for life. Riley's death was preventable, and the federal government knew exactly who Ibarra was.

Her case is not an anomaly. It is the predictable result of a system that identifies criminal aliens and then releases them. ICE's non-detained docket is the roster of removable aliens the agency is not holding. As of July 21, 2024, that roster included 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, among them 13,099 with homicide convictions and another 1,845 awaiting trial on homicide charges. In plain terms, 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities.

Every line of that docket is a policy choice. The alien was identified. The conviction is on the books. The removal authority exists. What is missing is detention capacity and the will to use it. Congress sets ICE's detention capacity in annual appropriations, so every murderer on that docket rather than in a bed is a decision made in Washington, not an accident of the system. The agency does not need new statistics to act on this docket. It needs the funding and the mandate.

## 2. Federal sentencing

The same story is written in federal sentencing data. More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the individuals sentenced that year, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7%, were illegal aliens. Another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable from the country.

Two-thirds of these noncitizen offenders, 65.9%, came from Mexico, followed by Honduras (8.7%) and Guatemala (5.8%). Illegal aliens are not a rounding error in the federal criminal caseload. They are more than a third of it, and each of those sentences stands for a crime with a victim. A noncitizen who reaches a federal sentencing hearing has already been arrested, charged and convicted in an American courtroom. Removal at that point should be automatic. Instead, criminal aliens complete their sentences, cycle back into communities and reappear on dockets like the one described above.

These figures count federal convictions only. The state caseloads are larger, and one state keeps the records that allow the public to see them clearly.

## 3. State data: Texas

Texas is the only state that systematically records immigration status in its criminal justice data, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety records the best available window on illegal alien crime at the state level. The view is grim. From June 1, 2011, through Sept. 30, 2026, Texas booked more than 466,000 criminal noncitizens into its jails. More than 335,000 of them were classified by DHS as illegal noncitizens, and they were charged with more than 603,000 criminal offenses, including 1,134 homicide charges, 79,089 assault charges, 7,713 sexual assault charges, 10,669 burglary charges, 1,547 kidnapping charges and 70,672 drug charges. Those charges have so far produced more than 230,000 convictions, including 636 homicide convictions.

DPS describes its own numbers as thousands of crimes that should not have occurred and thousands of victims who should not have been victimized because the perpetrator should not be here. The agency also notes that its counts include only aliens whose fingerprints were already on file with DHS, which means the true totals are higher.

The data themselves show how much higher. Texas has identified more than 11,000 illegal noncitizens only after they were already behind bars, too late for any detainer to matter, and that group alone carries 156 homicide charges and 120 homicide convictions. Analysts at the Center for Immigration Studies, examining the same Texas records, conclude that these identification delays understate illegal alien criminality even now, and that illegal immigrants are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the general population. Texas DPS data are the floor, not the ceiling.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers

How does a convicted criminal alien stay out of ICE custody long enough to reoffend? Ask the sanctuary jurisdictions. A detainer is ICE's request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours after a scheduled release so that federal officers can take custody. Sanctuary policies order local jails not to comply. In calendar 2025, jurisdictions across the country declined 17,864 ICE detainers, according to DHS testimony to Congress in March 2026.

New York is the case study. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, the state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers. The criminal charges and convictions associated with those refusals total 52,503, including 131 homicide charges and convictions, 1,017 sexual offenses, 1,776 robberies and 9,502 assaults. In December 2025, ICE's acting director wrote to New York's attorney general that sanctuary policies had freed nearly 7,000 criminal illegal aliens, including murderers and sexual predators. DHS has documented the results: a Queens murder and arson case in which the city's Department of Correction refused a detainer, and a Huntington rape case involving a 16-year-old victim. Rather than change course, New York enacted a 2026 law barring local police departments from partnering with ICE.

Congress has answered once already. The Laken Riley Act, the first bill signed into law in 2025, requires the detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary or assaulting a law enforcement officer. It is named for a victim the system failed. It should not be the last such law.

## 5. Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund the detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate the detention capacity ICE needs to take custody of the 425,431 convicted criminals on its docket, with homicide and violent convictions first in line, and report back on the docket's size each quarter.
2. **Enforce detainer compliance.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers, and extend the Laken Riley Act's mandatory detention standard to illegal aliens charged with any violent felony.
3. **Expand 287(g).** ICE has signed 2,679 agreements with state and local law enforcement agencies across 38 states. Fund the program so that every willing agency can participate, and let states require their sheriffs to cooperate.
4. **Require public reporting.** Direct DHS to publish quarterly data on the non-detained docket, on detainers declined by jurisdiction, and on every release of a criminal alien from custody. What gets measured gets enforced.

The data in this brief are the government's own. The question before Congress is whether it will act on them before the next victim's name is written into law.

*Brett Kessler is Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy at the Founders' Square Institute. The data appendix to this brief (tables A1-A5) accompanies this publication.*

# EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, October 27, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET

# FSI Brief: 13,099 Convicted Murderers Are Free in American Communities

New Border Security & Public Safety brief compiles ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission and Texas DPS data on criminal aliens and public safety

**WASHINGTON (Oct. 27, 2026)** — The Founders' Square Institute today published Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. The brief shows that the federal government's own data document a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement.

ICE's non-detained docket holds 425,431 convicted criminals, among them 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions: 13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities. Noncitizens accounted for more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those offenders were illegal aliens. In Texas, illegal noncitizens booked into local jails have been charged with more than 603,000 crimes since 2011, including 1,134 homicide charges. Sanctuary jurisdictions declined 17,864 ICE detainers in 2025 alone. New York has refused to honor 16,070 detainers since January 2025, and 131 homicide charges and convictions are associated with those releases.

"These are not our estimates. They are the government's own numbers, and they show thousands of convicted killers and other criminals loose in American communities while Washington declines to detain and remove them," Kessler said. "Every figure in this brief has a victim behind it. Congress has the power to close this gap, and this brief shows where to start."

The brief calls on Congress to fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement funding on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program and require quarterly public reporting on criminal alien releases.

The Founders' Square Institute is a public-policy think tank based in Washington, D.C.
